scenarios.explanation: files needs two records because A and AAAA are different address families. The existing nameserver, web and database records remain useful and must survive the edit. Saving changes the stored zone; only reload changes what the primary serves.
hints: A and AAAA are separate records at the same full name; one cannot replace the other.
Append the two files records rather than replacing the whole zone. Keep its NS and existing host lines.
Save the zone, then reload the primary. Use A and AAAA lookups to compare the served values.
scenarios.simplifications: Offline bounded forward-DNS resource-record editor and in-memory authoritative copies. Full names end in a dot; explicit decimal TTL and IN are required. A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/apex NS only; SOA serial is edited separately. No full BIND grammar/configuration/utilities, host zone files, caching, recursion, reverse/PTR, delegation/glue, transfer packets/timers, DNSSEC/TSIG or real DNS/mail/network activity. dns_teaching.prerequisite_note: Start here: no DNS or shell-command knowledge is assumed. Address values are supplied; this workspace edits only a simulated zone.

concepts.title: Give a name an address
concepts.text: DNS lets a readable name stand for data such as a computer address. A zone is the part of DNS you manage. A records hold IPv4 addresses; AAAA records hold IPv6 addresses. All addresses for this exercise are supplied; you do not need to calculate subnets. NS identifies the nameserver responsible for this zone. Its target ns.workshop.test. has its own A address line; keep both existing lines.

concepts.title: Write one complete record per line
concepts.text:
Type in Resource records. For example: files.dual-practice.test. 300 IN A 192.0.2.140. The name ends with a dot so it is complete. 300 is the TTL in seconds, how long a resolver may cache the answer; caching is not simulated here. IN means Internet class. An IPv6 example is a separate line:
files.dual-practice.test. 300 IN AAAA 2001:db8::140
Keep both A and AAAA records at the same name.

concepts.title: Saved is different from served
concepts.text: Save zone stores your edit inside this simulation. Reload primary makes that saved zone available to lookups. SOA serial is the zone revision number; increase it when editing. Look up with type A, then AAAA, checks the primary copy. Check configuration evaluates the whole assignment.

dns_teaching.example_description: In dual-practice.test., add files with A 192.0.2.140 and AAAA 2001:db8::140. Preserve web, db and ns. The worked example fills this practice editor only; save and reload it yourself.
dns_teaching.try_change: Change only the practice host IPv4 address, save without reloading, and compare its A lookup before and after reload.

guide.action: Use the native record editor and served-copy lookups. The Introduction and separate practice example can be reopened without losing assignment work.

scenarios.explanation: The failure is a cycle in names, not a missing subnet or an IPv4 calculation. Redirecting one edge to app ends the loop; the other alias can follow that path. Both canonical addresses and unrelated records stay in place. Direct A replacement would lose the requested alias relationship.
hints: Inspect the portal and status CNAME lines; following either currently returns to a name already visited.
Break the cycle by pointing one existing alias toward app. The other may continue through it.
Keep the A and AAAA records on app. Copying its number into portal as A does not keep portal as a CNAME alias.

concepts.title: A second name for one host
concepts.text: A CNAME record redirects a name to another name, not an IP address. The destination that owns the final A/AAAA records is the canonical host. For example, portal.alias-practice.test. 300 IN CNAME app.alias-practice.test. lets an A lookup follow the name to its address.

concepts.title: Follow the path, not just the number
concepts.text: Look up CNAME to inspect one alias target; look up A to follow the supported in-zone path. If two aliases point back to each other, no address is reached: the simulator reports Servfail and names the loop. Matching address text alone does not repair the intended host relationship.

concepts.title: Repair one link and verify both names
concepts.text: Use the existing record editor, Save zone and Reload primary. A CNAME name cannot also hold ordinary A/AAAA data. Preserve the canonical host records and test each requested alias. A valid intermediate alias is allowed; a direct copied A record is not this task.

dns_teaching.example_description: In alias-practice.test., portal and status loop. Repair both CNAME paths to app, whose supplied addresses are 192.0.2.160 and 2001:db8::160. Keep legacy and the nameserver.
dns_teaching.try_change: Point the practice status alias to itself, save/reload and inspect an A lookup. Repair it again without changing the app addresses.

scenarios.explanation: The primary MX targets mx-a directly at preference 10; the backup targets mx-b at preference 20. Each target owns an address record. A mail-alias CNAME cannot substitute for the canonical MX target. The old loaded answer can mask a bad saved configuration until publication is attempted.
hints: Compare the saved MX target with the CNAME line. MX must name the canonical mx-a host directly.
mx-b needs its own A record as well as the backup MX record.
Preserve the complete two-member MX set and web/nameserver data; then save and reload the primary.

concepts.title: How mail finds a host
concepts.text: MX records name mail hosts and a preference number. A smaller number is preferred. For example: mail-practice.test. 300 IN MX 10 mx-a.mail-practice.test. The exchange is a full host name, not an IP address.

concepts.title: A target also needs an address
concepts.text: An in-zone mail host needs its own A or AAAA record. MX/NS targets must be canonical names rather than CNAME aliases. Here the intended mail host names and IPv4 addresses are supplied. Repair both the MX target and any missing host address; an MX line alone is insufficient.

concepts.title: The old primary can still answer
concepts.text: The saved copy contains a problem, while the primary still holds the prior loaded records. Read the editor and try reload: in this simulator invalid alias targets leave the primary unchanged with a specific diagnostic. Repair, save and reload, then query MX and each host A. This proves DNS data only, not mail delivery. Real BIND has configurable warning/failure policy; this editor is not a full BIND loader.

dns_teaching.example_description: In mail-practice.test., repair the same kinds of saved-zone faults. Use MX 10 mx-a / MX 20 mx-b, with A 192.0.2.125 and 192.0.2.126. Keep web at 192.0.2.20 and ns.
dns_teaching.try_change: Change practice MX preferences to 30 and 5 and query MX after publishing. Notice which number is smaller; this simulator does not send mail.

hints: An A query must contain both active addresses and no retired one. Inspect all returned rows.

Preserve api and ns, save and reload before checking the served set.

concepts.title: One name can have several records
concepts.text: Records with the same name and type form a resource record set (RRset). A lookup may return more than one A address. For web.rrset-practice.test., the active addresses are 192.0.2.110 and 192.0.2.111. Both are needed; deleting one good line is not a safe cleanup.

concepts.title: Preserve other kinds of data
concepts.text: The AAAA record at that same name is a separate set. Another host name is separate again. Inspect the complete current A output and remove only the retired member; preserve the IPv6 and peer-host lines.

concepts.title: Order is not a delivery promise
concepts.text: Case, record order and exact duplicate rows do not create new DNS data. This simulator sorts output consistently for inspection; it does not model client address selection, balancing, caching or failover. Compare all members, then use Check configuration.

dns_teaching.example_description: In rrset-practice.test., remove web A 192.0.2.99 but retain A 192.0.2.110 / 192.0.2.111, AAAA 2001:db8::110, api and ns.
dns_teaching.try_change: Add an exact duplicate of one active practice A line and compare the served lookup. Then remove the duplicate again; record order does not define client delivery order.

Keep api.branch.test. at 203.0.113.20 and the nameserver records. Choose a newer SOA serial, publish and update without reverting the primary to the old address.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Compare served copies and repair revision-controlled publication.
guide.action: Use the native record editor and served-copy lookups. The Introduction and separate practice example can be reopened without losing assignment work.

scenarios.explanation: The secondary correctly ignores an equal serial even when the primary data changed. A newer saved serial must first become the loaded primary revision before the secondary can accept it. Copying the old answer back to the primary would agree on the wrong result; explicit address outcomes prevent that false pass.
hints: Query web on Primary and Secondary. The equal serials do not describe equal data in this exercise.
Do not change the primary back to the old address. Increase the saved serial from its current value.
Save zone, Reload primary, then Update secondary. Compare the new served A answer on both copies.
scenarios.simplifications: Offline bounded forward-DNS resource-record editor and in-memory authoritative copies. Full names end in a dot; explicit decimal TTL and IN are required. A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/apex NS only; SOA serial is edited separately. No full BIND grammar/configuration/utilities, host zone files, caching, recursion, reverse/PTR, delegation/glue, transfer packets/timers, DNSSEC/TSIG or real DNS/mail/network activity. TTL values are retained but prescribed TTL choices are not graded. Serial comparison uses unsigned32-bit DNS arithmetic; exactly half-range differences are diagnosed as undefined.

dns_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on the earlier forward-DNS lessons. The editor, absolute record syntax and save/reload workflow are reused; new ideas are explained below. Prerequisites are guidance, not a lock.

concepts.title: Two servers can hold different copies
concepts.text: A primary publishes the saved zone. A secondary keeps another copy for availability. Select Primary or Secondary before an A lookup to compare their answers. A matching name does not prove both have the same revision.

concepts.title: A revision number controls the update
concepts.text: SOA serial is the zone revision number. A primary can load changed data with an equal serial, but the secondary then sees no newer revision and retains its copy. For ordinary small changes, increase the saved serial, save, reload the primary and update the secondary. Any supported newer value is accepted; no particular decimal format is required.

concepts.title: Verify the new value and the peers
concepts.text: Check web on both copies, and preserve api/ns. This explicit Update secondary control models only the serial decision and copy, not DNS transfer packets or refresh timers. Advanced serial wraparound limits are available in the optional references.

dns_teaching.example_description: In secondary-practice.test., primary web is 203.0.113.180 and secondary web is 203.0.113.18 at equal serials. Publish a newer revision while retaining api and ns.
dns_teaching.try_change: First try Update secondary with the equal serial and compare both A lookups. Then increase the serial and follow save → reload → update.

Keep api at 192.0.2.50, archive at 192.0.2.90 and the existing nameserver records. Bring primary and secondary to the same current saved zone and verify the secondary portal answer.

guide.why: Combine host, alias, mail and secondary verification without losing peers.
guide.action: Use the native record editor and served-copy lookups. The Introduction and separate practice example can be reopened without losing assignment work.

scenarios.explanation: The handover changes the intended app/mail addresses and MX priority, preserves useful peers and keeps portal linked to app. Publishing a newer primary revision and then updating the secondary makes the saved and served copies agree. A copied portal A, wrong canonical host, lost peer, missing MX target address or stale secondary is incomplete even when one lookup looks right.
hints: Separate the task into host addresses, alias relationship, mail records and data to preserve. Keep the entire assignment available while editing.
MX preference 10 belongs to mail and 20 to backup. Both hosts need their own supplied A addresses.
Use a newer serial, save/reload the primary and update the secondary. Verify the secondary portal A; do not delete api, archive or ns to simplify the zone.

concepts.title: Use the earlier record skills together
concepts.text: This handover combines A/AAAA, CNAME paths, MX preference/canonical targets, preservation and primary/secondary publication. All target names and addresses are supplied. Start by comparing the current records with the full assignment; use lookups to inspect served evidence rather than replacing the zone blindly.

concepts.title: Choose a safe publication order
concepts.text: Repair the editor draft, keep unrelated api/archive/ns data, choose a newer serial and save. Reload primary validates the saved records and publishes them. Repair any reload diagnostic before updating the secondary. A successful primary lookup alone does not finish a two-copy handover.

concepts.title: Verify relationships, not only numbers
concepts.text: Keep portal as an alias to app, and keep mail/backup as hosts with their own address records. Query the secondary portal A and the zone MX set. The assignment checks the entire current state; a later harmful edit or an unsaved divergent draft removes current completion.

dns_teaching.example_description: Practice the handover in handover-practice.test. with app A 198.51.100.110 / AAAA 2001:db8:1::110, mail 198.51.100.35 and backup 198.51.100.36. Keep portal as an alias, MX 10 mail / MX 20 backup and the supplied api/archive/ns data.
dns_teaching.try_change: After a successful practice handover, make one unsaved alias edit and observe why current checks need a saved, published configuration. Retry after restoring the intended relationship.
